properties.doc: What the chart is of — "Revenue by month". A chart is the one thing on a screen a reader gets nothing from: the shapes carry all of it, and the numbers behind them are the caller's. A name and a `Figure` role are the least that makes it navigable, and they are not the whole answer — see the note in `docs/reference/accessibility`.

name: heatmap
summary: Charts: a scale, its ticks, and a line or area drawn from data.
signatures: HeatmapResult heatmap(Ui& ui, const Interaction& input, std::string_view id, const std::vector<std::vector<double>>& values, const HeatmapOptions& options = {});
notes: A grid of cells shaded by value. `values` is row-major and may be ragged — a short row simply has fewer cells, which is what a calendar's last week is. The colour is one token at varying strength rather than a rainbow. A multi-hue scale looks richer and reads worse: hue carries no order, so a reader has to consult the legend for every cell, while "more of the same colour" needs no legend at all.

properties.name: rows
properties.doc: Names down the side and along the top. Fewer than there are rows or columns leaves the rest unlabelled rather than renumbering them.

properties.name: columns
properties.doc: As above, along the top.

properties.name: steps
properties.doc: Quantise the colour into this many steps; zero is a continuous ramp. Five by default, and steps rather than a ramp because a reader compares cells by *matching* them, not by judging absolute lightness. Two cells one step apart are visibly different; two cells 3% apart on a continuous ramp are the same colour to anyone reading a grid at a glance.

properties.name: color
properties.doc: The hue the scale runs to. Unset takes the design's first chart colour, so the grid re-themes with everything else.

properties.name: cellSize
properties.doc: Zero lets the cells share out the width.

properties.name: rowLabels
properties.doc: Room for the labels. Zero draws none.

properties.name: columnLabels
properties.doc: The same, along the top.

properties.name: name
properties.doc: What the chart is of — "Revenue by month". A chart is the one thing on a screen a reader gets nothing from: the shapes carry all of it, and the numbers behind them are the caller's. A name and a `Figure` role are the least that makes it navigable, and they are not the whole answer — see the note in `docs/reference/accessibility`.

name: lineChart
summary: Charts: a scale, its ticks, and a line or area drawn from data.
signatures: ChartResult lineChart(Ui& ui, const Interaction& input, std::string_view id, const std::vector<Series>& series, const ChartOptions& options = {});
ChartResult lineChart(Ui& ui, const Interaction& input, std::string_view id, const std::vector<Series>& series, ChartView& view, const ChartOptions& options = {}, const ChartZoom& zoom = {});
notes: Draws one or more series over a shared scale. The geometry is built here and handed to `Ui::draw`, so the whole chart is one node plus its labels rather than a widget per mark. Hit testing is on the *index* — the pointer's x is turned back into a sample number — which is what lets a tooltip name the right point instead of the nearest pixel.

The same chart, showing only `view` of the data and letting the reader move it. The view is the caller's, like every other piece of state here — which is what lets two charts share one, so panning a line chart pans the bars under it.

properties.name: scale
properties.doc: Fixed bounds. Left as they are, the chart takes them from the data — which is what a live readout wants and what a comparison does not.

properties.name: tickCount
properties.doc: Each of these falls back to `Design::chart` when it is not set, so a dashboard configures its charts once instead of per call site.

properties.name: axisWidth
properties.doc: Room for the value labels down the left. Zero draws none.

properties.name: hover
properties.doc: A crosshair and a readout following the pointer.

properties.name: valueFormat
properties.doc: Printed beside a hovered value; "%.0f" style, as `std::snprintf` takes.

properties.name: categories
properties.doc: Names for the samples, used as the readout's heading.

properties.name: link
properties.doc: Ties this chart's readout to the other charts sharing the same `ChartLink`, so pointing at a sample in one points at it in all of them. Null leaves the chart on its own.

properties.name: legend
properties.doc: The key drawn under the chart, and the focus a click on it gives.

properties.name: name
properties.doc: What the chart is of — "Revenue by month". A chart is the one thing on a screen a reader gets nothing from: the shapes carry all of it, and the numbers behind them are the caller's. A name and a `Figure` role are the least that makes it navigable, and they are not the whole answer — see the note in `docs/reference/accessibility`.

name: radarChart
summary: Charts: a scale, its ticks, and a line or area drawn from data.
signatures: ChartResult radarChart(Ui& ui, const Interaction& input, std::string_view id, const std::vector<Series>& series, const RadarOptions& options = {});
notes: One value per axis, per series, on spokes around a common centre. The chart for a *profile* — a handful of measures that belong together and are compared as a shape rather than read off one at a time: a skills assessment, a wine's tasting notes, one machine's five utilisation figures against another's. Everything it is good at falls apart past about eight axes, where the polygon stops being a shape and becomes a scribble. `series` is the same `Series` every other chart here takes; each value is a spoke, in order, starting at twelve o'clock and going clockwise. Hit testing is by *angle*, so a reader pointing anywhere along a spoke means that axis — the same rule the bars use for a category, for the same reason.

properties.name: scale
properties.doc: Fixed bounds. Left alone the chart takes them from the data — and always from zero, whatever the data says. A radar is read as an *area*, and area from a non-zero baseline is the same lie a truncated bar tells, told about five axes at once: two profiles a hair apart become one enormous and one tiny.

properties.name: categories
properties.doc: One name per axis, drawn outside its spoke. Fewer than there are values leaves the rest unlabelled rather than renumbering them.

properties.name: size
properties.doc: The whole chart's box, labels included.

properties.name: grid
properties.doc: What is drawn behind the data: a mesh, shaded bands, or nothing.

properties.name: labelRoom
properties.doc: Room between the outermost ring and the edge, for the names. Zero draws none and gives the web the whole box.

properties.name: fillAlpha
properties.doc: Shading inside a series' polygon, when the series carries no `fillAlpha` of its own. Filled by default, where a line chart is not. A line is read along, and shading under two of them buries the lower one; a radar is read as a shape, and an unfilled one is a wire outline the eye has to close for itself. Lower than the 0.2 the web charting libraries settle on, and deliberately: the painter composites in linear light, where the same number covers roughly twice as much as it does in a browser blending sRGB directly.

properties.name: markerRadius
properties.doc: A dot at each vertex. Zero draws none.

properties.name: valueFormat
properties.doc: Printed in the readout; "%.0f" style, as `std::snprintf` takes.

properties.name: name
properties.doc: What the chart is of — "Revenue by month". A chart is the one thing on a screen a reader gets nothing from: the shapes carry all of it, and the numbers behind them are the caller's. A name and a `Figure` role are the least that makes it navigable, and they are not the whole answer — see the note in `docs/reference/accessibility`.

name: scatterChart
summary: Charts: a scale, its ticks, and a line or area drawn from data.
signatures: ScatterResult scatterChart(Ui& ui, const Interaction& input, std::string_view id, const std::vector<PointSeries>& series, const ScatterOptions& options = {});
notes: Points on two continuous scales — a scatter, or a bubble chart when the points carry weights. The first chart here with a real **x scale**. Every other one indexes its samples along the bottom: sample 0 at the left, sample n at the right, evenly spaced whatever their x values are. That is right for a series over time and wrong for a correlation, where the whole question is where the points sit against each other on both axes. Hit testing is by distance to the nearest dot rather than by column, because a scatter has no columns — two points can share an x and mean different things.

properties.name: xScale
properties.doc: Fixed bounds for each axis. Left alone, both come from the data.

properties.name: yScale
properties.doc: As above, for the other one.

properties.name: xFormat
properties.doc: The same, for the x value. Two formats because the axes are two different quantities — seconds against dollars.

properties.name: xAxis
properties.doc: Room under the plot for the x labels. Zero draws none.

properties.name: minRadius
properties.doc: The radii the weights are spread across, when there are weights.

properties.name: fillAlpha
properties.doc: How solid a dot is. Under one on purpose: overlapping points then read as denser rather than hiding each other, and density is most of the information in a crowded scatter.

properties.name: hitRadius
properties.doc: How near the pointer has to be, in pixels, to pick a dot.

properties.name: name
properties.doc: What the chart is of — "Revenue by month". A chart is the one thing on a screen a reader gets nothing from: the shapes carry all of it, and the numbers behind them are the caller's. A name and a `Figure` role are the least that makes it navigable, and they are not the whole answer — see the note in `docs/reference/accessibility`.
